title: The Elegant Flirt 1
content:
The Lan Clan’s mountain estate lay tucked deep in the ranges beyond Gusu city.

Winding pavilions, serene courtyards, and whitewashed walls with dark-tiled roofs drifted under a perpetual mantle of mountain mist. Walking through it felt like wandering into an ethereal sea of clouds. In the hush of the early dawn, a milky haze swallowed the ridges, matching its name to perfection: The Cloud Recesses.

Quiet mountains, quiet souls; a stillness so deep it was like water in a frozen well. Only the measured, distant chime of an alpine bell rippled from a high tower—not a Buddhist sanctuary, yet steeped in that solitary, meditative chill.

Naturally, that tranquil zen was ripped to shreds by a prolonged, deafening wail.

A collective shudder ran through the rows of disciples halfway through their dawn drills and scripture recitals. Necks craned instinctively toward the front gates.
 
There was Wei Wuxian, clutching the spotted donkey around its neck and weeping like his heart was breaking.

Lan Jingyi threw his hands up in sheer exasperation. “What are you crying for?! You’re the one who blabbed that you liked Hanguang-jun! Now that he’s actually brought you home, what the hell are you howling about?!”

Wei Wuxian’s face remained crumpled in pure misery.

After that circus of a night on Dafan Mountain, he hadn’t found a single spare second to summon Wen Ning again, let alone figure out why the guy had lost his marbles, or how on earth he had walked back among the living in the first place. Before he could even catch his breath, Lan Wangji had hauled him off like a sack of turnips.

Back when he was a teenager, Wei Wuxian had spent three agonizing months boarding here with the other clan heirs, so he knew down to his bones just how soul-crushingly dull the Gusu Lan Sect really was. He still had nightmares about the Wall of Discipline, whose sheer rock face was crammed with over three thousand micro-carved rules. Dragged up the mountain path this morning, he had stolen a glance at the stone out of morbid curiosity—only to discover they’d chiseled on another thousand! Four thousand rules. Four!

“Enough!” Lan Jingyi snapped. “Zip it! No clamoring inside the Cloud Recesses!”

I’m only yelling this loud because I don’t want to go inside, you little brat!

Once they dragged him past those wards, breaking back out was going to be a nightmare. In his school days, guest disciples had each carried a jade passage token; you had to keep it on your hip just to cross the perimeter without getting fried. Thirteen years down the line, their security was definitely tighter, not looser.

Lan Wangji stood by the grand entrance, deaf to the theatrical wailing, watching with cool, detached eyes. The second Wei Wuxian ran out of breath and let the volume dip, Lan Wangji dropped his verdict: “Let him cry. When he tires, drag him in.”

Wei Wuxian tightened his death grip on the donkey and redoubled his fake tears, thumping his forehead against the poor beast's neck in despair.

Talk about shooting yourself in the foot! He’d assumed taking a lash from Zidian would scrub away every shred of suspicion. Riding that wave of smug relief—and saddled with a loose tongue that couldn't resist clowning around—he had tossed out that shameless lie just to gross Lan Wangji out. Who could’ve guessed Lan Wangji wouldn't play by the old rules? What was the logic here? Had a decade of spiritual transcendence somehow shrunk the guy's petty heart instead of broadening it?

Wei Wuxian raised his chin, shouting, “I prefer men, you know! Your clan is crawling with drop-dead gorgeous guys—what if I can't keep my hands to myself?!”

Lan Sizhui stepped in, trying to be the voice of reason. “Young Master Mo, Hanguang-jun brought you along for your own protection. If you hadn't come with us, Sect Leader Jiang wouldn't have let you off the hook. Over the years, countless people have been hauled into Lotus Pier for interrogation, and not a single one ever walked back out.”

“He’s right,” Lan Jingyi chimed in. “You haven’t had a taste of Sect Leader Jiang's methods, have you? Utterly vicious…” Catching himself badmouthing an elder, he froze, nervously glancing sideways at Lan Wangji. Seeing no thunder gathering on Hanguang-jun’s brow, the boy dared to grumble on: “It’s all the Yiling Laozu’s fault for starting this rotten trend. Half the world copies his shady tricks instead of doing honest cultivation, and Sect Leader Jiang jumps at every shadow. Can he really kidnap everyone? And please, look at you—playing the flute like a dying pig… Hah.”

That parting scoff dripped with enough condescension to drown an army. Wei Wuxian felt deeply compelled to defend his honor: “Look, you probably won't believe me, but normally my flute playing is actually quite—”

Before he could finish digging his own grave, several figures in white emerged from the inner courtyard.

They wore the signature pristine Lan robes, their sashes fluttering with quiet elegance. Leading the group was a tall, jade-poised gentleman; slung at his waist beside a masterwork sword was a vertical xiao flute carved from pure white jade. At his approach, Lan Wangji dipped his head in greeting. The newcomer mirrored the bow, turning his gaze upon Wei Wuxian with a gentle smile: “Wangji never brings guests home. Who might this be?”

Standing face-to-face with Lan Wangji, the resemblance was like looking into a silver mirror. The only difference lay in their eyes: while Lan Wangji’s irises were a pale, glassy amber, this man’s gaze held a softer, deeper warmth.

It was Lan Huan, Zewu-jun—Clan Leader Lan Xichen.

Gusu's misty valleys had always had a reputation for churning out striking beauties, and this generation’s Twin Jades of Lan were the crown jewels. Though not identical twins, their features were nearly ninety percent identical, making it impossible to crown one prettier than the other. But their presence was entirely distinct: Lan Xichen was gentle as a spring breeze, radiating approachable grace, whereas Lan Wangji stood as aloof and unbending as an ice floe, keeping the mortal world at arm's length. Naturally, when the clans ranked the most eligible young masters, Lan Xichen took the top spot, leaving his brother at number two.

True to his stature as a great clan leader, Lan Xichen didn’t even twitch an eyebrow at the sight of a grown man glued to a braying farm donkey. Grinning ear-to-ear, Wei Wuxian let go of the animal and strode forward. The Lan clan worshipped seniority and etiquette; all it took was a few crude, outrageous lines tossed at Lan Xichen, and the disciples would beat him down the mountain with wooden paddles. But just as he opened his mouth to work his magic, Lan Wangji cut a sharp glance his way—and Wei Wuxian’s lips instantly snapped shut, glued tight by the Silence Spell.

Lan Wangji turned back, continuing his deadpan report: “Is Brother heading out to meet Lianfang-zun?”

Lan Xichen nodded. “To finalize the arrangements for the upcoming Discussion Conference at Carp Tower.”

With his jaws clamped shut, Wei Wuxian could only slink back to his donkey in defeat.

Lianfang-zun was none other than Jin Guangyao, the current master of the Lanling Jin Sect—the only bastard Jin Guangshan had ever officially acknowledged. He was Jin Ling's young uncle, the half-brother of Jin Ling’s late father, Jin Zixuan—and, by extension, the half-brother of this body's previous owner, Mo Xuanyu. Both illegitimate sons, yet worlds apart: Mo Xuanyu had slept on freezing mud eating kitchen scraps, while Jin Guangyao sat at the apex of the cultivation world commanding the wind and rain, pulling Lan Xichen into private talks and hosting conferences whenever he pleased. Then again, it was hardly a surprise the two clan leaders were thick as thieves; they were sworn brothers, after all.

“Uncle took the relic you brought back from Mo Village to examine,” Lan Xichen added.

The words Mo Village piqued Wei Wuxian’s ears. Suddenly, the tightness in his face eased; Lan Xichen had casually waved a hand to break the Silence Spell, turning to his brother with a gentle chide: “It's rare for you to bring someone home, let alone in such high spirits. Treat your guest with proper courtesy; don’t behave like this.”

High spirits?! Wei Wuxian squinted, staring hard at Lan Wangji’s stone-cold mug.

Where on that deadpan face do you see ‘high spirits’?!

Once Lan Xichen’s silhouette faded into the pines, Lan Wangji turned his cool gaze back to the courtyard. “Drag him in.”

And so, Wei Wuxian was physically hauled across the threshold he had once sworn to the heavens he would never cross again.

The Cloud Recesses usually entertained only distinguished dignitaries; they’d certainly never seen a specimen like this before. The disciples nudged and steered him along, treating the spectacle like an amusing field trip; if the rules hadn't hung over their heads, the trail would’ve echoed with barely contained snickers.

Lan Jingyi called out, “Hanguang-jun, where should we take him?”

“The Jingshi.”

“…The Jingshi?!”

Wei Wuxian blinked in confusion, but the boys traded stunned, wide-eyed glances, abruptly swallowing their tongues.

That was Hanguang-jun’s personal study and private bedchamber—a sanctuary where no living soul was ever allowed to set foot...

The interior of the Jingshi was austere, stripped of any superfluous clutter. A finely painted folding screen caught the shifting play of light with delicate brushwork clouds, sitting neatly behind a low guqin table. Off in the corner, a tripod incense burner carved from white jade puffed faint, curling ribbons of mist, filling the room with that crisp, solitary scent of cold sandalwood.

Lan Wangji had marched off to confer with his uncle on clan business, leaving Wei Wuxian shoved inside. Naturally, the second Lan Wangji’s front foot cleared the threshold, Wei Wuxian’s back foot slipped right out behind him. He took a brief recon stroll through the Cloud Recesses only to run into the expected reality: without a passage jade, trying to vault the soaring white walls simply triggered the barrier ward, bouncing you straight onto your rear and alerting every patrol in a mile radius.

Sighing, Wei Wuxian had no choice but to wander back to the Jingshi.

He had never been one to sweat over sticky situations. Clasped hands behind his back, he paced across the floorboards, confident he’d sniff out an exit eventually. The clean sandalwood aroma hung thick in the air—chilly, detached, yet weirdly magnetic. He caught his mind wandering: Lan Zhan always carries this scent. He must spend so much time practicing his zither and meditating in here that the smoke gets baked into his robes.

Trailing the thought, he drifted closer to the incense burner in the corner. As his boot came down, one particular floorboard felt noticeably different under his weight. Curious, he dropped into a crouch and began tapping rhythmically around the boards. Having spent half his past life digging trenches, desecrating tombs, and burrowing into secret tunnels, it took him less than a breath to pry the loose plank up.

Finding a secret stash inside Lan Wangji’s room was mind-boggling enough, but taking in its contents nearly blew Wei Wuxian’s lid off.

With the board set aside, an intoxicating, mellow fragrance cut through the sandalwood. Tucked neatly into a small square cellar below were seven or eight plump, pitch-black jars.

Lan Wangji really had changed—the man was hoarding booze!

Alcohol was strictly forbidden in the Cloud Recesses; in fact, that exact rule was why the two of them had come to blows the very first night they met, with Lan Wangji smashing a jar of Emperor’s Smile he’d smuggled up the mountain from Gusu city.

After returning to Yunmeng, Wei Wuxian had never found another chance to taste Gusu’s famous brew. It had remained a lifelong itch; he had always told himself he’d slip back one day for a sip, but life got in the way. Yet here it was. Without even pulling a stopper, the aroma told him everything he needed to know: Emperor's Smile, without a doubt. To think that Lan Wangji—the living paragon of moral rigidity who wouldn't touch a drop of liquor to save his life—had hollowed out a secret cubby under his floorboards to hoard wine. Truly, karma had a wicked sense of humor.

Wallowing in nostalgia, Wei Wuxian knocked back an entire jar. He’d always had a bottomless tolerance and a shameless craving for good drink; considering Lan Wangji had owed him a jar all these years, he figured charging a little interest was only fair, so he popped open a second. Halfway through the second jug, lightning struck.

Why break his head over an escape when the token was so obvious?

The Cloud Recesses housed a Cold Spring tucked away in the crags, renowned for its miraculous properties—clearing the mind, soothing the spiritual pathways, and purging internal fires for male disciples during cultivation. And when you soaked in a spring, you had to strip. Unless someone planned to hold their jade passage token between their teeth, it’d be sitting right there on the rocks!

Wei Wuxian clapped his hands, downing the last dregs. Realizing he couldn't just chuck the ceramic outside, he topped both empty jars with clean water, sealed them back up, stuffed them into the hole, and hammered the plank flat. Chores finished, he slipped out into the fog to hunt for a token.

Even though the Cloud Recesses had been burned to the ground prior to the Sunshot Campaign, its reconstructed layout mirrored the original down to the inch. Navigating the winding garden paths from muscle memory, he soon found his way to the secluded hollow sheltering the Cold Spring.

The guards posted along the perimeter were spaced far apart. The female cultivators had their own secluded sectors and never set foot here, and no upright Lan disciple would ever dare commit the shameless crime of peeping on their brothers. With security so relaxed, slipping past was child's play—practically an open invitation for Wei Wuxian to get up to no good. Better yet, draped across a flat white boulder beyond the iris beds lay a neatly folded set of robes. Someone was already inside.

The white fabric was folded with maddening precision, sitting on the rock like a square block of snow, the forehead ribbon tucked flat without a single wrinkle. Slipping his fingers inside to fish for the jade, Wei Wuxian almost felt guilty messing up the crisp lines. Parting the tall stalks of grass, his gaze drifted lazily toward the water—and froze.

The spring was piercingly cold, with none of the warm, obscuring steam of a bathhouse to cloud the view. The bare upper torso of the bather was exposed in pristine, crystalline clarity, back turned to the bank.

He was tall and lithe, his pale skin striking against the dark current, wet black hair swept neatly over one shoulder. The lines of his back were lean and sculpted—graceful, yet carrying a quiet, terrifying strength. In short, a gorgeous specimen.

Yet Wei Wuxian didn’t freeze because he was struck dumb by a handsome bather; he wasn't into men anyway. What pinned him to the dirt was the horrific tapestry carved across that pale back.

Dozens of deep, crisscrossing scars.

The marks of a discipline whip. In the great sects, that barbed lash was reserved exclusively for disciples who had committed unforgivable, catastrophic crimes. Once delivered, the scars were permanently burned into the spiritual core, never to fade. Wei Wuxian had never tasted the whip himself, but Jiang Cheng had. No matter what rare salves they applied, that mark of shame refused to lighten by a fraction; Wei Wuxian could never mistake the branding.

Normally, taking one or two lashes was enough to set a man straight for the rest of his natural life. Yet carved across this back were at least thirty overlapping strikes. What brand of treasonous heresy could earn a punishment that savage? And if his crime had truly been that unforgivable, why hadn’t the clan simply cleaned house and ended him on the spot?

Right then, the man shifted in the water, turning around.

Just beneath his left collarbone, resting right over his heart, was the scorched, unmistakable outline of a brand.

Taking in the shape of that scar, Wei Wuxian felt the breath vanish from his lungs.
